questions.q: How strong is gravity on the surface of Mars?
questions.do: Mars is picked when the page opens. Look at the NASA fact sheet table and read the row Surface gravity.
questions.a: 3.7 m/s², which is 0.38 × Earth. A person would weigh a bit more than a third of their Earth weight.

questions.q: Which needs a bigger total change in speed from Earth orbit: landing on the Moon or landing on Mars?
questions.do: Under Pick a world, click Moon and read Total from Earth orbit in the Sending a Starship table. Then click Mars and read the same row.
questions.a: The Moon needs 6.25 km/s; Mars needs only 4.34 km/s. Mars is much farther away, but its air does most of the braking (the landing step is just 0.75 km/s). On the airless Moon, the ship must burn 3.10 km/s to stop and land.

questions.q: What is the heaviest payload one refilled Starship could land on Titan?
questions.do: Click Titan. Read the last row, Most payload a refilled Starship could carry. Then move the Payload to the surface slider from 50 t to 100 t and watch the verdict.
questions.a: About 81 t. At 50 t the verdict says Possible (about 1,318 t of propellant). At 100 t it says Not in one ship, because the propellant needed is more than the 1,550 t tank holds.

questions.q: Mercury is much closer to us than Mars. Why does the lab say a Starship could not land on Mercury in one go?
questions.do: Click Mercury. Compare Arrival speed relative to the target and the row Braking burn all the way down, no air with the same rows for Mars.
questions.a: Mercury needs 16.61 km/s in total, so the verdict is Not in one ship. Falling in towards the Sun, the ship arrives very fast (9.61 km/s relative to Mercury), and Mercury has no air. So the engines must cancel all of it: 11.06 km/s of braking.

questions.q: The lab can show the sky of Aryabhata's time. How far apart were Earth and Mars on that date, and how does it compare with the day of Apollo 11?
questions.do: In the orrery, click the Aryabhata, 499 CE button and read the line Earth to Mars on this date. Then click Apollo 11 and read it again.
questions.a: About 335 million km in 499 CE, but only about 88 million km on the Apollo 11 date (1969). Both planets go round the Sun at different speeds, so the gap between them keeps changing.
